title: Hunting a leak
sub: Two snapshots, the difference and the path to a root
cards/0/title: The method: two snapshots and a diff
cards/0/body:
A leak in .NET is not "forgot to free" but "someone still holds a reference". The GC will not collect an object while there is a path to it from a root. The job is to find what grows and who holds it.

  • Make sure it is a leak: the floor of the sawtooth rises under steady load (lesson 1).
  • Warm the service up so caches and the JIT have done their work, and take snapshot A.
  • Run a known number of operations: say, 1000 requests.
  • Take snapshot B and compare it with A.
  • Pick a type whose instance count grew by about 1000 or a multiple of it, and find the path from a root to any of its instances.
cards/0/deep: Pick a round, noticeable number of operations so the growth is recognizable: +1000 objects for 1000 requests is clearly "one per request". A dotnet-gcdump snapshot performs a full collection itself, so garbage does not get into the diff. A full dump keeps the garbage, so in dotnet-dump count with dumpheap -stat -live — reachable objects only.
cards/1/q: Put the steps of a leak hunt in order
cards/1/items/0: See in the counters that the heap after full collections keeps growing
cards/1/items/1: Warm the service up and take the first snapshot
cards/1/items/3: Take the second snapshot and compare it with the first
cards/1/items/4: For the type that grew, find the path to a root
cards/1/items/5: Fix it and repeat the same snapshots
cards/1/explain: First you confirm the problem, then you get a diff under a known load, then you look for who holds it. The last step is the same measurement after the fix: the growth should be gone.
cards/2/body:
In a snapshot comparison (Visual Studio, PerfView) every type has a growth in instance count and in size.

  • Look at the count, not only the size. At the top by size there are almost always string and byte[] — they are leaves; something holds them.
  • Look for your own types: OrderSnapshot, Session, ViewModel. They are closer to the cause than the strings inside them.
  • Tell an object’s own size (exclusive) from its retained size (inclusive) — everything that would die along with it. A small dictionary can retain a gigabyte.
cards/2/deep: Retained size is computed from the dominator tree: object X dominates Y if every path from the roots to Y goes through X. PerfView and Visual Studio build this tree approximately — the heap graph is reduced to a spanning tree, and an object reachable by two paths has its size attributed to one of them. That is why "inclusive" can differ between tools.
cards/3/q: After 1000 requests the snapshot diff is: +1000 OrderSnapshot, +3000 string, +1000 byte[], and one List<OrderSnapshot> grew. Where do you start?
cards/3/options/0: With OrderSnapshot: find the path to a root and see whose list it is
cards/3/options/1: With string: there are the most of them
cards/3/options/2: With byte[]: the arrays take the most space
cards/3/explain: The strings and arrays are most likely fields of OrderSnapshot: three strings and an array per order snapshot. Your own type growing by exactly one per request plus a growing list is direct evidence. Warm-up was done before the first snapshot.
cards/4/body:
Roots (GC roots) are where the collector starts its walk:

  • static fields — alive as long as their type, usually the whole life of the process;
  • local variables and arguments on thread stacks that will still be used;
  • GC handles: strong, pinned — created by GCHandle.Alloc, the runtime and libraries;
  • the finalization queue — objects waiting for a finalizer are temporarily alive.

The retention path is the chain of references from a root to the object. gcroot in dotnet-dump and the paths view in Visual Studio and PerfView give it to you. Read top to bottom and look for a link that should not be there.
cards/4/deep: An event subscription is a reference from the publisher to the subscriber: the delegate stores in its _target field the object whose method will be called. So a long-lived publisher holds everyone who subscribed and never unsubscribed. System.Threading.Timer is a special case: the runtime’s timer queue holds the callback, but not the Timer object itself. If nothing references the Timer, it gets collected and stops; the leaking timer is one kept in a long-lived place and never stopped. An async method awaiting a task that never completes holds its state machine through that task’s continuation.
cards/5/q: The OrderWindow was closed long ago, but gcroot shows it is alive. Which link should not be there?
cards/5/explain: PriceFeed is a long-lived service; it is supposed to live. But its event holds a delegate, and the delegate holds the closed window: the window subscribed to PriceChanged and did not unsubscribe on close. The fix is to unsubscribe in Closed or Dispose.
cards/6/body:
• Events. A short-lived object subscribed to an event of a long-lived one and never unsubscribed.
  • Static collections and caches without eviction. A static Dictionary as a "cache" that is only ever added to. Or a MemoryCache without a SizeLimit and expirations.
  • Timers. A timer in a long-lived object that nobody stopped: it holds the callback, and the callback holds this.
  • Closures. A lambda stored for a long time holds everything it captured — sometimes the whole object via this.
  • Registrations on a long-lived token. token.Register(...) on an application-wide token without disposing the registration.
cards/6/deep: A closure captures variables, not values, and the compiler puts all captured variables of a method into one closure object. If two lambdas in a method captured different variables and one of them lives long, it holds both. Another old source is thread-local data ([ThreadStatic], ThreadLocal<T>) on thread-pool threads: the threads live long, and the data lives with them.
cards/7/q: Which of these causes a leak in a long-running service? Select all.
cards/7/options/0: static readonly Dictionary<string, Report> Cache that is only ever added to
cards/7/options/1: A request handler subscribes to an event of a singleton service and never unsubscribes
cards/7/options/2: A local List<T> inside a method, filled with a million items
cards/7/options/3: Every request adds a lambda that captured this to a static List<Action>
cards/7/options/4: An array rented from ArrayPool and given back with Return
cards/7/explain: The static dictionary, the singleton’s event and the static callback list outlive the request and hold everything they reference: a lambda with this holds the whole handler. The local list dies when the method returns, and the pooled array went back to the pool — that is reuse, not a leak.
cards/8/body:
• A stuck finalizer thread. Finalizers run on a single thread. If someone’s finalizer waits on a lock or goes to the network, the queue grows, and objects with finalizers — and everything they hold — are not freed. The sign: finalizequeue shows thousands of objects ready for finalization.
  • Fragmentation. Few live objects, but a big heap: buffers pinned for a long time prevent compaction. Look at FragmentedBytes and gchandles.
  • Native memory behind small wrappers — lesson 1.
cards/8/deep: You can see the finalizer thread in a dump: clrthreads shows it marked Finalizer, and clrstack for it shows where it is stuck. Finalizers must not block, and resources are better released through Dispose than left to a finalizer. Long pinning is a typical trace of old code with fixed or GCHandle.Alloc(..., Pinned) held for the whole run; for long-lived buffers .NET 5+ has the POH: GC.AllocateArray<T>(n, pinned: true).
cards/9/q: The heap grows. In a dump, finalizequeue shows 400,000 objects ready for finalization, and the finalizer thread’s stack is sitting in Monitor.Enter. What is going on?
cards/9/options/0: Some finalizer is waiting on a lock, and the whole finalization queue is stuck
cards/9/options/1: The garbage collector is turned off
cards/9/options/2: The objects have too many fields
cards/9/options/3: This is expected: finalizers always run at process exit
cards/9/explain: There is one finalizer thread. While it waits on a lock, new objects pile up in the queue and stay alive with everything they hold. The fix is to remove the lock from the finalizer and release resources through Dispose.
cards/10/body:
After the fix, repeat the same measurement: warm-up, snapshot, 1000 requests, snapshot. The growth of your type should drop to zero.

To keep the leak from coming back, write a test. Create the object in a separate method, hand back a weak reference (WeakReference), run a collection and check that the object is dead.

The separate method with NoInlining matters: in a Debug build the JIT extends the lifetime of locals to the end of the method, and an object created in the test itself may survive the collection.
cards/10/deep: Put GC.WaitForPendingFinalizers() between two GC.Collect() calls: the first collection finds the garbage, the finalizers run, the second removes what finalizable objects were holding. Do not run such tests in parallel with others that allocate heavily — the result gets flaky. There are libraries with memory assertions too, but their mechanism is the same.
cards/11/q: Finish the test: a closed window must not stay in memory
cards/11/explain: A collection, waiting for finalizers, another collection — then check IsAlive. Target would return the object itself, while Assert.False expects a bool. KeepAlive would do the opposite and extend the object’s life.
